extracted.intended_audience: readers of humorous fiction / P. G. Wodehouse enthusiasts
extracted.subtask_description: Passage from a P. G. Wodehouse comic novel (Psmith, Journalist). Contains dialogue, situational comedy, and a few embedded normative remarks about literary practice and practical precautions for journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor who believes in the novice
rubrics_metrics.description: “what the novice chiefly needed was an editor who believed in him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psmith cites treatises on 'How to Succeed in Literature' saying belief from an editor is the chief need of a novice; he expresses that finding such an editor (in Billy Windsor) is crucial to a newcomer's success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative stimulus from risk or adversity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Men such as ourselves, Comrade Windsor, need a certain stimulus, a certain fillip, if they are to keep up their high standards. The knowledge that a low-browed gentleman is waiting round the corner with a sand-bag poised in air will just supply that stimulus. Also that fillip. It will give our output precisely the edge it requires.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psmith argues (tongue-in-cheek) that danger or the prospect of interruption can sharpen a writer's output; presented as a normative claim about what maintains the 'edge' of literary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for complete quiet to produce best work
rubrics_metrics.description: “Your literary man must have complete quiet if he is to give the public of his best.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psmith worries that daytime intrusions (e.g., gang members dropping into the office) would prevent good work; this motivates the satirical plan to hire a fighting-editor to keep interruptions away — an implicit guideline about the working conditions required for quality journalism/literary production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fighting-editor selection criteria (physical toughness over charm)
rubrics_metrics.description: “We want a man of thews and sinews, a man who would rather be hit on the head with a half-brick than not. And you, Comrade Brady, are such a man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the qualities desired for a fighting-editor: physical robustness and willingness to take punishment are valued far above charm or genteel manners. Psmith contrasts 'charm of manner' with the practical requirements of the post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use publicity/patronage to create reciprocal obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: “'But for _Cosy Moments_,' he should be saying to himself, 'where should I be? Among the also-rans.' I imagine that he will do any little thing we care to ask of him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psmith reasons that promoting or helping someone (here, Kid Brady's career) generates gratitude that can be called upon later; presented as a pragmatic tactic for securing favors or protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kindness yields reciprocal goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative example: Comrade Windsor restored a cat to Comrade Jarvis instead of making soup of it; as a result Comrade Jarvis refused to take a contract against Windsor and is favorably disposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit moral/practical guideline: acts of kindness (even small ones) can produce loyalty and favours from others; used in the text to explain why Bat Jarvis declined to do harm.
